newsitem.title: UK: UK launches studies for new bomber aircraft.
newsitem.headline: UK launches studies for new bomber aircraft.

text.p: Britain said on Monday that it is to commission a 35 million pound ($58.07 million) study into its options for replacing its Tornado GR4 ground attack jets.
Defence procurement minister James Arbuthnot told Parliament that the Ministry of Defence expects to place the necessary study contracts in the new year.

One of the options being considered by the Royal Air Force (RAF) is a new version of the four-nation Eurofighter but defence officials said recently they were also considering buying the U.S.'s planned new Joint Strike Fighter as well as looking at unmanned vehicles and stand-off missiles.

"Options to be examined include variants of the Eurofighter and other new design and off-the-shelf combat aircraft, unmanned air vehicles and stand-off air-to-ground missiles launched from transport aircraft," Arbuthnot said.
The Ministry of Defence said in a statment that the scope for collaboration within Europe and elsewhere "would be fully explored."

Eurofighter is due to become Britain's main combat aircraft after the year 2002 but the RAF wants to replace the Tornado strike and reconnaissance aircraft with a Future Offensive Aircraft (FOA) by about 2015.

A mid-life upgrade (MLU) programme being undertaken by British Aerospace to overhaul and equip the current fleet of 142 Tornado GR4s with new capabilities got underway in April this year, with the first converted aircraft due to go into service in March 1998 and the last in 2002.

British defence officials said recently that the MLU would keep the RAF's Tornado strike capability going well into the first decade of the next century but by 2015, each aircraft will probably have flown for some 9,000 hours, more than twice their original design life.
Initial studies for the Ministry of Defence for the FOA were completed at the end of 1995 and one option looked at was a longer range strike version of Eurofighter.
A derivative of the Eurofighter could keep the new aircraft affordable and British Aerospace has drawn up a design for a thicker wing to increase fuel capacity.

According to British defence sources, other options to be looked at will be various one and two-seat aircraft including stealth designs, as well as ideas for unmanned air vehicles (UAVs) and for using large aircraft from which to launch a volley of smart cruise missiles.
But the sources say the RAF favours a conventional manned aircraft and discussions have been held with potential partner countries, including France, Germany and the U.S. ($1=.6027 Pound)
